k-1.x_notes: Five problems on four pages, all on actual-size outlines (1-inch edges checked). They are: sailboat and cat with any pieces; hexagon and side-2 diamond each filled two different ways; arrow and six-point star with chevrons only; long hexagon with blues only and then any pieces; side-3 triangle with greens and then any pieces. I checked the constrained ones: the arrow takes 2 chevrons, the star 3 and the long hexagon 5 blues, so none is broken. The page is concrete with real variety, from free filling to 'two different ways' to single-piece constraints, and there is enough here for 40 minutes. Weaknesses: the cat is small and quick. 'Ask an adult to trace your pieces' and 'Use them again for the next shape' are small procedural extras. Nothing asks children to notice or compare anything (for example how many blues the diamond took compared with greens).
k-1.y_notes: Two problems: fill the sailboat with any pieces, then cover the side-3 triangle with greens and count them (9). Both are correct and at actual size. That is roughly five to ten minutes of work for the 40-minute block, with most of each page blank. There is no 'different ways', no constraint and no comparison. This is the organizer's exact complaint: a K-1 page that is too dumbed down and ends far too early.
k-1.reason: Y gives the K-1 children two trivial fills and leaves them with nothing to do for most of the session. X has five concrete, correctly built puzzles with a sensible progression that will keep them busy.

grades-2-3.x_notes: Problem 1 is four boards to fill with blues. Problem 2 is triangles with sides 2 through 5, finding the best blue packing; the fewest gaps is always n (2, 3, 4, 5), and the page ends with 'compare your four best packings… explain why you cannot leave fewer'. Problem 3 is six boards done first with blues, then with chevrons. I checked them: A 0/0, B 0/4, C 0/0, D 0/2, E 1/1, F 2/4 empty for blues/chevrons. That is a good contrast set: F has even area but the blues still leave 2, and chevrons are never better than blues. It ends with 'can you cover a purple with blues?', which carries the kernel through to the chevron argument. All boards are actual size and the work fills the session. Weaknesses: the two impossible boards in Problem 1 (A and C) have an odd number of triangles, so the first 'what stops you' has a trivial answer and the even-area surprise waits until Problem 3 F. The 'Problem 2:' label and its directions are repeated on page 3. The 'Fewest empty… Blues/Purples' recording line is a little ambiguous. The last question leans toward the answer.
grades-2-3.y_notes: These are exactly X's first two pages and stop there. Problem 2 still says 'and the triangle on the next page', but there is no next page. The side-5 triangle, the compare-and-explain prompt and the whole chevron problem are missing. The impossible boards in Problem 1 have odd area, so without the missing prompt nobody is asked why the triangles leave n gaps. That is about 15 to 20 minutes of work for four third graders, and the central explanation never arrives. Fixing it in 15 minutes would mean writing the missing pages.
grades-2-3.reason: Y is a truncated copy with a dangling reference to a page that does not exist. It drops the explanation question and the chevron problem, which is the heart of kernel 1, and the group would run out of work early. X contains everything in Y plus a well-chosen, correct contrast set that carries the argument through.

grades-4-5.x_notes: Ten problems on a hexagon with side lengths 1, 2 and 2, which has exactly 6 rhombus tilings. Problem 1 builds every tiling on a 1-inch board, with recording boards. Then come the flip map on cards A to F, the shortest route from A to F (4 flips), and the odd-return question. Problems 5 to 8 cover ribbons: drawing them, why each has 2 L and 2 R, listing all 6 orders and matching them to cards (which proves the count is 6), and rebuilding a tiling from a ribbon. Problems 9 and 10 cover flips as swaps of an adjacent LR pair. I decoded every drawn tiling. The cards are valid and all different (A RRLL, B RLRL, C LRRL, D RLLR, E LRLR, F LLRR). The A-to-B flip example is a genuine single flip, and the pre-drawn ribbons on A and in Problem 8 are correct. This is the complete development of kernel 2, and the page will not run out. Weaknesses: there are many small numbered steps. Problems 3, 4 and 9 are short, and Problem 10's 'circle every LR/RL' prints most of the discovery. The parity argument is never tied back explicitly to Problem 4. It is probably more than 40 minutes, but the later problems work as extension.
grades-4-5.y_notes: These are X's Problems 1 to 5 word for word, so everything present is correct and well built. Tilings, flip map, shortest route and the odd-return question make a decent session. The page stops just after introducing ribbons on A and B, so ribbons never get used to count the tilings or to explain the flip parity, and the most interesting part of the kernel is cut off. Strong 4th and 5th graders could finish this before the 40 minutes are up.
grades-4-5.reason: Both are correct, and Y is an adequate session. But Y cuts off right after ribbons are introduced, so Problem 4's parity question and the count of 6 tilings get no explanation. X carries the ribbon idea through to both and gives the strong 4th and 5th graders enough to work on.

overall.reason: Y is X truncated in every band. Its K-1 page is two trivial fills, its grades 2-3 page refers to a missing page and drops the explanation and the chevron problem, and its grades 4-5 page stops before ribbons pay off. X is correct throughout (every board, packing bound and tiling diagram checked), concrete and at actual size, and fills the hour in all three groups. Its main flaws are some over-directed small steps in grades 4-5, and fifteen minutes is enough to trim those.
